definition: To regard with disgust and hatred
example: Most people abhor cruelty to animals in any form.
origin: From Latin abhorrere “to shrink back from in horror”, from ab- “away from” and horrere “to bristle, to shudder”.

definition: To warn or criticize someone firmly but gently
example: The coach had to admonish two players for arriving late.
origin: From Old French amonester, from Latin admonere “to remind, to warn”, from ad- “to” and monere “to warn”.

definition: To mention something in an indirect way
example: She likes to allude to her years in Paris without giving details.
origin: From Latin alludere “to play with, to jest”, from ad- “to” and ludere “to play”.

definition: To calm someone by giving what they demand
example: The manager offered a refund to appease the angry customer.
origin: From Old French apaisier “to bring to peace”, from a- “to” and pais “peace”, from Latin pax.

definition: To charm someone, sometimes in order to deceive
example: The salesman tried to beguile us with stories of easy profits.
origin: From be- “thoroughly” and guile “deceit”, from Old French guile, of Germanic origin.

definition: To ask for something in an anxious, urgent way
example: I beseech you to think again before you sign that contract.
origin: From Middle English besechen, from be- (intensive) and sechen “to seek”, from Old English secan.

definition: To think about something deeply and at length
example: He sat by the lake to contemplate his future.
origin: From Latin contemplari “to gaze at, to observe”, from con- (intensive) and templum, a space marked out for watching omens.

definition: The feeling that something deserves no respect
example: She looked at the cheap souvenirs with obvious disdain.
origin: From Old French desdeign, from desdeignier “to scorn”, from Latin dedignari “to reject as unworthy”, from de- “away” and dignari “to deem worthy”.

definition: To ask someone earnestly or anxiously
example: Let me entreat you once more to stay until morning.
origin: From Old French entraiter “to treat, to deal with”, from en- and traiter “to treat”, from Latin tractare “to handle”.

definition: To praise highly or raise in rank
example: The poem seems to exalt the simple life of the countryside.
origin: From Latin exaltare “to raise high”, from ex- “out, upward” and altus “high”.

definition: To beg someone desperately to do something
example: Doctors implore the public to stay home during the storm.
origin: From Latin implorare “to call upon with tears”, from in- “upon” and plorare “to weep, to cry out”.

definition: To grow weak or remain neglected for a long time
example: Thousands of applications languish in a queue for months.
origin: From Old French languiss-, stem of languir, from Latin languere “to be faint, to be weak”.

definition: To confuse and worry someone
example: The strange results perplex the scientists who ran the experiment.
origin: From the older adjective perplex “confused”, from Latin perplexus “entangled”, from per- “thoroughly” and plectere “to weave, to braid”.

definition: To criticize someone sharply for what they did
example: The judge did not hesitate to rebuke the lawyer for his rudeness.
origin: From Anglo-French rebuker “to beat back”, from re- “back” and Old French buschier “to strike, to chop wood”, from busche “log”.

definition: Blame or criticism for a fault or failure
example: His mother's eyes were full of silent reproach.
origin: From Old French reproche, from reprochier “to blame”, probably from Latin re- “back” and prope “near”: to bring something back close to someone.

definition: To refuse to accept or be connected with
example: The senator was quick to repudiate the remarks of his own adviser.
origin: From Latin repudiare “to divorce, to reject”, from repudium “divorce, rejection”.

definition: To suppose something is true without firm proof
example: From the empty driveway I surmise that they have already left.
origin: From Old French surmis, past participle of surmettre “to accuse”, from sur- “upon” and mettre “to put”.

definition: To annoy, worry or frustrate someone
example: Small delays vex him far more than real disasters ever do.
origin: From Old French vexer, from Latin vexare “to shake, to harass, to trouble”.

definition: To be unsteady or unable to decide
example: Her support for the plan began to waver after the first setback.
origin: From Middle English waveren, probably from Old Norse vafra “to flicker, to move unsteadily”.

definition: Great enthusiasm or passion
example: They defended their small theater with surprising ardor.
origin: From Old French ardour, from Latin ardor “heat, flame”, from ardere “to burn”.

definition: Extreme greed for money or possessions
example: His avarice cost him every friend he ever had.
origin: From Old French avarice, from Latin avaritia, from avarus “greedy”, from avere “to crave”.

definition: A sudden, unpredictable change of mood or behavior
example: The schedule seemed to change at the caprice of the director.
origin: From French caprice, from Italian capriccio “a sudden start, a shiver”, perhaps from capo “head” and riccio “hedgehog”: a head with the hair standing on end.

definition: The state of being calm and in control
example: She kept her composure even when the audience began to shout.
origin: From compose and the suffix -ure; compose comes from Old French composer “to put together”, from com- “together” and poser “to place”.

definition: Courage shown through pain or long difficulty
example: She bore the long illness with remarkable fortitude.
origin: From Latin fortitudo “strength”, from fortis “strong”.

definition: Anger at something that seems unfair or wrong
example: The decision to close the school caused widespread indignation.
origin: From Latin indignatio, from indignari “to regard as unworthy”, from in- “not” and dignus “worthy”.

definition: A deep, lasting and thoughtful sadness
example: A gentle melancholy settled over him as the summer ended.
origin: From Greek melankholia, from melas “black” and khole “bile”; an excess of black bile was once thought to cause sadness.

definition: A state of pleasant, dreamy thought
example: The ringing phone pulled her out of her reverie.
origin: From French rêverie, from rêver “to dream”, in Old French “to wander, to be delirious”, of uncertain origin.

definition: A moral doubt that makes you hesitate
example: He had no scruple about reading other people's letters.
origin: From Latin scrupulus “a small sharp stone”, hence a source of unease, from scrupus “rough stone”.

definition: A loud, confused noise or state of disorder
example: The speaker could not be heard above the tumult of the crowd.
origin: From Latin tumultus “commotion, uproar”, related to tumere “to swell”.

definition: Too much pride in your looks or achievements
example: Out of vanity, he refused to wear his glasses in public.
origin: From Old French vanité, from Latin vanitas “emptiness, worthlessness”, from vanus “empty”.

definition: Physical or mental strength and energy
example: At eighty she still argues with the vigor of a young lawyer.
origin: From Old French vigor, from Latin vigor “liveliness”, from vigere “to be lively, to thrive”.

definition: Severe mental or physical pain
example: The families waited in anguish for news of the rescue.
origin: From Old French anguisse “a choking sensation”, from Latin angustia “narrowness, distress”, from angustus “narrow”.

definition: The wish to harm or upset other people
example: There was no malice in his joke, only clumsiness.
origin: From Old French malice, from Latin malitia “badness, ill will”, from malus “bad”.

definition: A false reason given to hide the real one
example: He left the meeting early on the pretext of a headache.
origin: From Latin praetextus “outward show”, from praetexere “to weave in front, to disguise”, from prae- “before” and texere “to weave”.

definition: Care and concern for someone's comfort or wellbeing
example: The nurse treated every patient with the same quiet solicitude.
origin: From Latin sollicitudo “anxiety”, from sollicitus “agitated, troubled”, from sollus “whole” and citus “set in motion”.

definition: A person's face or its expression
example: His cheerful countenance put the nervous visitors at ease.
origin: From Old French contenance “bearing, behavior”, from Latin continentia “restraint”, from continere “to hold together”.

definition: Friendly and pleasant to be with
example: Our amiable neighbor always stops to chat over the fence.
origin: From Old French amiable, from late Latin amicabilis “friendly”, from Latin amicus “friend”.

definition: Needing great effort; difficult and tiring
example: The arduous climb to the summit took nearly twelve hours.
origin: From Latin arduus “high, steep, difficult”.

definition: Quick to understand a situation and gain from it
example: An astute observer would have noticed the tension in the room.
origin: From Latin astutus “crafty, clever”, from astus “craft, cunning”.

definition: Distant and not friendly or involved
example: He remained aloof from the office gossip and ate lunch alone.
origin: From a- “on” and loof, an old form of luff “the windward side of a ship”; a ship kept aloof stayed clear of the shore.

definition: Very sad and without hope
example: She grew despondent after her third job application was rejected.
origin: From Latin despondere “to give up, to lose heart”, from de- “away” and spondere “to promise”.

definition: Causing fear or respect by being large or powerful
example: The champion faces a formidable opponent in tonight's final.
origin: From Latin formidabilis, from formidare “to fear”, from formido “fear, terror”.

definition: Proud and looking down on other people
example: The haughty waiter ignored us for nearly half an hour.
origin: From Middle English haut “high, proud”, from Old French haut “high”, from Latin altus.

definition: Acting quickly without thinking about the results
example: His impetuous decision to quit left the family without income.
origin: From Latin impetuosus, from impetus “attack, rush”, from impetere “to attack”.

definition: So foolish or unreasonable as to be laughable
example: It is ludicrous to expect the work to be done by Friday.
origin: From Latin ludicrus “sportive, done in play”, from ludere “to play”.

definition: Silently bad-tempered and gloomy
example: The sullen teenager answered every question with a shrug.
origin: From Anglo-French solein “alone, solitary”, from Old French sol “alone”, from Latin solus.

definition: Showing strong and forceful feeling
example: The plan met with vehement opposition from local residents.
origin: From Latin vehemens “violent, eager, impetuous”, of uncertain formation.

definition: Full of gentle, sad longing
example: She gave a wistful smile as the train pulled away.
origin: Probably from the obsolete wistly “intently”, with its sense of longing influenced by wishful.

definition: Rude and not showing proper respect
example: The reporter was told that his question was impertinent.
origin: From late Latin impertinens “not belonging, not to the point”, from in- “not” and pertinere “to pertain”.

definition: So beautiful or grand as to inspire awe
example: The view from the top of the pass was simply sublime.
origin: From Latin sublimis “uplifted, lofty”, probably from sub “up to” and limen “lintel”.

definition: Gloomy and depressing, or very bad
example: Ticket sales were dismal during the long, wet summer.
origin: From Anglo-French dis mal, from medieval Latin dies mali “evil days”, the unlucky days of the medieval calendar.

definition: Too ready to believe what you are told
example: Credulous investors lost millions in the scheme.
origin: From Latin credulus “easily believing”, from credere “to believe”.

definition: Quiet and easy to control or teach
example: The horse was docile enough for a child to ride.
origin: From Latin docilis “easily taught”, from docere “to teach”.
